rationale: An established open specification for exactly the kind of structured dataset metadata (schema, provenance, licensing) needed to determine a dataset's suitability for training, which is RQ10's question.

Standardizes dataset metadata (provenance, licensing, responsible-AI fields, record/field structure) in a machine-readable form adopted by Hugging Face, Kaggle, OpenML and Google Dataset Search, which is exactly the infrastructure needed for researchers to audit large datasets without bespoke per-dataset parsing.

Defines the structured metadata (schema, licence, provenance, ML-semantics layer) a consumer needs to judge a dataset's fitness for training -- a second, independently-adopted standard alongside frictionless-data-package answering the same question.

SPDX 3.0's AI profile (AIPackage) defines a standard schema for licence and metadata reporting on AI systems -- training/fine-tuning data references, data preprocessing, sensitive-data usage, standard-compliance documentation -- which is precisely the licence/metadata reporting requirement RQ7 asks about.

As a machine-readable bill-of-materials format, SPDX 3.0 lets each stage of the AI value chain (data, training, model, deployment) declare and cross-reference its dependencies and provenance, forming the audit-registry substrate RQ59 asks for; complements opsml's registry implementation with the underlying interchange standard.

Generates fresh, semantically-equivalent non-deterministic variants of benchmark problems on the fly rather than reusing a fixed static set, which is exactly the mechanism RQ32 asks for: independent evaluation against a standardised task without needing to openly host the evaluation dataset.

Presidio's entity-recognition engine scans a corpus and reports which PII/sensitive-data types are present, which is a direct instance of verifying that a dataset does (not) include certain kinds of information -- RQ45's question -- independent of its existing use for downstream log redaction (RQ40).

ScanCode's standardized, automatable license-detection scan across a codebase/dataset is a concrete formalisation of the process RQ47 asks about -- verifying correct use of licensed data -- complementing its existing role scanning for license *presence* (RQ2/RQ3) by applying the same scan against a *stated* licence-compliance requirement.

Zero-knowledge proof of inference lets a model owner demonstrate compliance/correctness properties to a third party without disclosing weights or architecture, which is precisely the reconciliation RQ39 asks for between research/auditing access and commercial or safety confidentiality concerns.

Purpose-built to sign and verify cryptographic provenance manifests for ML models at each stage of the value chain (data, training, release), which is a direct implementation of an audit-registry mechanism for end-to-end verification -- RQ59's question -- distinct from its existing RQ3 role checking license accuracy across aggregated datasets.

The same DP mechanisms that let diffprivlib reconcile data access with privacy-preserving ML (RQ30) also structure third-party analysis so it preserves privacy while enabling meaningful auditing -- RQ29's question -- since noised/aggregated statistics are exactly the auditing primitive being asked for.

MPC lets multiple parties jointly compute over data none of them individually discloses, which structures third-party dataset access to preserve privacy while still enabling meaningful joint auditing -- RQ29's question -- via a different technique than diffprivlib's differential privacy, complementing rather than duplicating it.

Identifying which model produced a given output from black-box-accessible artifacts (embeddings) is directly usable to detect an unauthorized duplicate or stolen model in the wild, which is RQ38's question about how different access levels affect the risk of model theft/duplication -- distinct from its existing RQ63 role verifying evaluated-vs-deployed model identity.

Tracing generated text back to specific training data points is direct evidence of whether a model was trained on a given dataset -- RQ44's question -- complementing membership-inference-based verification (ml-privacy-meter) with an attribution-based approach; distinct from its existing RQ12 role explaining behaviour generally.

Explainability algorithms that inspect data, local and global model behaviour require full access to the model, which is exactly the setting RQ54 asks about (verifying model properties with full access); complements its existing RQ21 role of mechanistic-analysis-for-understanding with a verification framing.

The general-purpose C2PA manifest implementation is the underlying provenance-chain building block audit registries need to provide end-to-end verification along the value chain (RQ59), alongside the ML-specific intellabs-atlas-cli which builds on the same standard for models specifically.

As an MPC library, JIFF reconciles data access with privacy-preserving machine learning (RQ30) the same way carbynestack does -- joint computation without raw data disclosure -- complementing its existing RQ43 role of cross-entity log analysis with the general privacy-preserving-ML case.

As a maintained benchmark for manipulation detectors' accuracy over time, IMDL-BenCo directly measures the robustness question RQ67 asks (how robust AI content detectors can be expected to be against advancing generative methods), complementing its existing narrower RQ68 role (genuine-but-edited image handling).

A taxonomy-classified catalogue of real incidents by sector/system type is direct empirical evidence for RQ94's question (what risks are associated with different types of systems), complementing its existing RQ95 role (how risks differ across domains) with the system-type framing.

Directly answers RQ85 by name: it is a model editing/unlearning framework with dedicated multilingual (CKnowEdit) and multimodal (MultimodalEditor over MiniGPT-4/BLIP-2/LLaVA-OneVision/Qwen2-VL) support, providing the substrate for measuring editing effectiveness across languages and modalities.
